data.text:
Hull off the Mare Island Navy Yard, California, United States, 20 Apr 1942

The USS Hull (DD-350) was a Farragut-class destroyer that served in the United States Navy during World War II. She was named after Commodore Isaac Hull, the famous commander of the USS Constitution during the War of 1812. The ship was launched in 1934 and commissioned in 1935, making her one of the newer destroyers in the fleet at the outbreak of the war.

Hull was stationed at Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941, when the Japanese attacked. She was moored in the navy yard for repairs and maintenance at the time, but her crew manned the antiaircraft guns and returned fire during the attack. She survived the day without major damage and subsequently participated in numerous operations throughout the Pacific theater.

Over the course of the war, Hull escorted convoys, screened carrier task forces, and provided shore bombardment support during various island-hopping campaigns. She participated in operations in the Aleutians, the Gilbert and Marshall Islands, the invasion of Tarawa, the Marianas campaign, and operations supporting the liberation of the Philippines. She earned ten battle stars for her World War II service.

Hull met a tragic end on December 18, 1944, when she was lost in Typhoon Cobra (also known as Halsey's Typhoon) in the Philippine Sea. The storm caught Admiral William Halsey's Third Fleet while it was refueling east of the Philippines, and the typhoon's extreme winds and massive waves overwhelmed several ships. Hull, along with destroyers Spence and Monaghan, capsized and sank in the violent seas. Of her crew of approximately 264 men, only 62 survived, rescued after spending many hours in the water. Her commanding officer, Lieutenant Commander James Alexander Marks, was among the survivors.

The loss of Hull and the other destroyers in Typhoon Cobra led to significant changes in naval weather forecasting and fleet procedures for handling severe weather. A subsequent Navy court of inquiry examined the disaster and its lessons influenced how the Navy prepared for and responded to tropical storms for the remainder of the war and beyond. It remains one of the worst non-combat disasters in U.S. Navy history.

There was also an earlier USS Hull (DD-7), a Bainbridge-class destroyer from the early 1900s, and a later USS Hull (DD-945) commissioned in 1958, but the Farragut-class DD-350 is the one most associated with World War II service.
